content: Acne vulgaris is a chronic dermatological condition characterized by the presence of inflamed lesions, blackheads, and, in severe cases, cysts and scarring. These lesions typically appear on the face, neck, back, and chest. Many individuals with acne seek complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) therapies, such as herbal remedies, acupuncture, and dietary changes, due to concerns about the side effects of conventional treatments. However, the efficacy and safety of these CAM therapies have not been systematically evaluated. To address this, a systematic review was conducted to assess the effects and safety of various CAM therapies in individuals diagnosed with acne vulgaris. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing CAM interventions to no treatment, placebo, or other active therapies. A total of 35 studies involving 3,227 participants were included. The methodological quality of these studies was generally unclear, with risks of selection, attrition, reporting, and detection biases noted. Due to clinical heterogeneity and incomplete data reporting, only four trials could be included in two meta-analyses. The CAM therapies evaluated included herbal medicine, acupuncture, cupping therapy, dietary interventions, purified bee venom (PBV), and tea tree oil. One trial was funded by a pharmaceutical company, while the funding sources for the other trials were not reported. The primary outcome of interest was the improvement in clinical signs of acne, assessed through changes in inflammatory and non-inflammatory lesion counts, total lesion counts, lesion scores, and acne severity scores. For dietary interventions, two studies compared low-glycemic-load diets (LGLD) with high-glycemic-load diets (HGLD) over 12 weeks. There was no clear evidence of a difference in non-inflammatory lesion counts between the groups (mean difference [MD] -3.89, 95% confidence interval [CI] -10.07 to 2.29, P = 0.10, 75 participants, low-quality evidence). However, one of these studies showed that LGLD reduced inflammatory lesions (MD -7.60, 95% CI -13.52 to -1.68, 43 participants) and total lesion counts (MD -8.10, 95% CI -14.89 to -1.31, 43 participants). Data from the other study were incomplete and could not be synthesized. Tea tree oil demonstrated potential benefits in a single trial, showing a reduction in total lesion counts (MD -7.53, 95% CI -10.40 to -4.66, 60 participants, low-quality evidence) and acne severity scores (MD -5.75, 95% CI -9.51 to -1.99, 60 participants). Similarly, a single trial on purified bee venom suggested it was more effective than control in reducing lesion counts (MD -1.17, 95% CI -2.06 to -0.28, 12 participants). The remaining 31 trials provided inconsistent results regarding the efficacy of acupuncture, herbal medicine, and wet-cupping therapy in reducing skin lesions or achieving remission. Adverse effects were reported in 26 of the 35 studies, but no severe adverse events were noted. Mild adverse effects were associated with herbal medicines, wet-cupping therapy, and tea tree oil gel. Two studies assessed quality of life and found significant improvements in self-worth and emotional functionality in favor of CAM therapies. However, none of the included studies evaluated psychosocial functioning. Overall, the evidence supporting the use of CAM therapies for acne vulgaris is limited and of low quality. While LGLD, tea tree oil, and bee venom showed some potential benefits in reducing total skin lesions, there is insufficient evidence to support the use of other CAM therapies, such as herbal medicine, acupuncture, or wet-cupping therapy. Mild adverse effects were reported, but the safety of these therapies requires further investigation. Future studies should aim to minimize bias, adhere to current clinical trial reporting standards, and provide more robust evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of CAM therapies for acne vulgaris.
